title: Optimal Water Level Management for Mitigating GHG Emissions through Water-Conserving Irrigation in An Giang Province, Vietnam
source_sections: 3.4. Relationships between Specific Water Management Practices and CH4 Emissions
4.2. Effect of Multiple Drainage on Rice Yield

key_claims.text: The researchers analyzed field datasets from six locations in An Giang, Vietnam, comparing continuous flooding with multiple drainage across seasons.
Methane emissions varied with water-management indicators; observed associations depend on field and seasonal conditions.
key_claims.source_section: 3.4. Relationships between Specific Water Management Practices and CH4 Emissions

key_claims.text: Field heterogeneity and limited sampling constrain how widely the yield findings can be generalized.
key_claims.source_section: 4.2. Effect of Multiple Drainage on Rice Yield

limitations: Paired field experiments across locations and seasons do not isolate every management or site factor.
The 3D soil scene is hypothetical and does not calculate methane emissions or yield.
learning_objectives: Describe the comparison and its geographic setting.
Explain how water management may affect root-zone conditions.
Distinguish an observed association from a universal causal prediction.

lesson_flow.title: Set the field question
lesson_flow.body: The study asks how irrigation management relates to rice yield and greenhouse-gas emissions in An Giang, Vietnam. Fields and seasons are not identical.
lesson_flow.check_question: Why record site and season as well as irrigation?

lesson_flow.title: Compare management
lesson_flow.body: The dataset includes continuous flooding and multiple-drainage management, with water levels monitored in farmers’ fields. This is a field comparison rather than a perfectly controlled laboratory experiment.
lesson_flow.check_question: Which other practices might also differ?

lesson_flow.title: Interpret methane
lesson_flow.body: The authors relate water-level indicators and non-flooded days to measured methane emissions. The relationships are evidence for those observed conditions, not a universal equation.
lesson_flow.check_question: Can an association alone establish the same effect at every farm?
lesson_flow.source_section: 3.4. Relationships between Specific Water Management Practices and CH4 Emissions

lesson_flow.title: Evaluate the limits
lesson_flow.body: Yield and emissions vary with management, soil and season; restricted sampling and irrigation availability limit direct transfer to another field.
lesson_flow.check_question: What additional measurements would improve a local decision?
lesson_flow.source_section: 4.2. Effect of Multiple Drainage on Rice Yield

questions.prompt: What was compared in the An Giang dataset?
options: Rice grown in pots at three fixed temperatures
Rice fields under continuous flooding and multiple drainage
Two nitrogen fertilizer rates under identical irrigation
questions.explanation: The paper compares water-management practices across field datasets.

questions.prompt: Why is a water-level association not automatically a universal causal law?
options: Seasons, fields and management can also differ
Every measured water level uniquely determines emissions
An association is proof of a universal mechanism
questions.explanation: Other varying conditions limit causal interpretation and generalization.
questions.source_section: 4.2. Effect of Multiple Drainage on Rice Yield

questions.prompt: What can the teaching scene tell you about methane?
options: The measured daily emissions of a selected farm
An exact methane emission calculated from water depth
How a changed water stage alters an illustrative soil scene, not actual emissions
questions.explanation: The scene is a conceptual illustration and contains no fitted methane model.
questions.source_section: 3.4. Relationships between Specific Water Management Practices and CH4 Emissions

visual_task: Compare the flooded, draining and drained views; then return to flooded to illustrate reflooding. Describe the visible water and roots. The diagram is fictional and does not predict yield or methane.

title: An assessment of irrigated rice cultivation with different crop establishment practices in Vietnam
source_sections: Site and crop descriptions, experimental design and water management

key_claims.text: Four rice-establishment methods were compared in farmer fields in Can Tho over two growing seasons.
key_claims.source_section: Site and crop descriptions, experimental design and water management

key_claims.text: Researchers used quadrats after establishment to quantify planting uniformity.
The paper reports differences in establishment, resource use and yield within its study conditions.

limitations: Different seasons used different fields and varieties, so outcomes must be interpreted in context.
Rows and broadcast in the teaching scene are stylized layouts, not recorded plant locations or yield predictions.
learning_objectives: Identify alternative establishment methods and the field design.
Explain how plant distribution can be measured.
Separate visual layout from evidence about yield and resource use.

lesson_flow.title: Compare methods
lesson_flow.body: Researchers compared manual broadcasting, blower broadcasting, drum seeding and mechanical transplanting in Can Tho rice fields.
lesson_flow.check_question: Which practices change seed placement?
lesson_flow.source_section: Site and crop descriptions, experimental design and water management

lesson_flow.title: Measure uniformity
lesson_flow.body: After establishment, the team counted plants in quadrats and compared variation in their distribution.
lesson_flow.check_question: Why use several quadrats rather than one plant?

lesson_flow.title: Read outcomes in context
lesson_flow.body: The study examined planting uniformity and measures including yield and resource use across two seasons. Different fields and varieties also varied by season.
lesson_flow.check_question: Why should the season and variety accompany a reported comparison?
lesson_flow.source_section: Site and crop descriptions, experimental design and water management

lesson_flow.title: Design a follow-up
lesson_flow.body: A new trial could repeat methods in multiple fields while recording seed rates, variety, water management and costs.
lesson_flow.check_question: What would replication add?

questions.prompt: Why did the researchers use several quadrats?
options: To estimate variation in plant distribution
To infer each plant’s eventual grain yield directly
To eliminate any difference among the fields
questions.explanation: Multiple sampling areas provide information about spatial variation.

questions.prompt: Can a neat row in the scene prove higher yield?
options: Yes, row spacing alone determines yield
Yes, the scene reproduces the authors’ harvested plots
No; yield must be measured under the study conditions
questions.explanation: The diagram is invented and does not compute harvest.

questions.prompt: Which factor matters when comparing the two seasons?
options: Only the number of sampled quadrats
The fields and varieties differed between seasons
Only the time between sowing and the first quadrat count
questions.explanation: Differences in conditions constrain direct comparisons.
questions.source_section: Site and crop descriptions, experimental design and water management

visual_task: Switch between rows and broadcast; compare spatial arrangement. These are invented layouts, not the paper’s plant counts or harvest results.

title: Organic farming practices change the soil bacteria community, improving soil quality and maize crop yields
source_sections: High-throughput sequencing of soil community bacteria

key_claims.text: The researchers compared maize production practices at a site in Brazil over two crop years.
They characterized soil bacterial communities using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing.
key_claims.source_section: High-throughput sequencing of soil community bacteria

key_claims.text: Yield and soil properties differed among management treatments in the studied setting.

limitations: Management treatments differ in several practices, so bacterial differences do not by themselves prove a microbial cause of yield differences.
Microbes in the 3D scene are symbolic, not species abundances or sequencing observations.
learning_objectives: Describe the comparison and sequencing measurement.
Distinguish microbial community composition from crop yield.
Explain why correlation is not enough to establish microbial causation.

lesson_flow.title: Study a farming system
lesson_flow.body: The researchers compared maize management practices at one Brazilian site across crop years, measuring soil and plants.
lesson_flow.check_question: Why is the site and management history relevant?

lesson_flow.title: Observe soil life
lesson_flow.body: They used bacterial 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing to compare community composition in soil samples. This measures sequence-based community patterns, not a direct crop-yield mechanism.
lesson_flow.check_question: Does finding a bacterial sequence prove what that organism caused?
lesson_flow.source_section: High-throughput sequencing of soil community bacteria

lesson_flow.title: Compare outcomes
lesson_flow.body: Soil properties, bacterial communities and yield differed across treatments. Weather and management also belong in the interpretation.
lesson_flow.check_question: Which measurements describe the soil and which describe the harvest?

lesson_flow.title: Reason about causality
lesson_flow.body: A controlled follow-up isolating microbial effects would be needed to establish whether particular microbes caused a yield change.
lesson_flow.check_question: What else changed between treatments?

questions.prompt: What does 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing help compare?
options: Grain moisture in each maize kernel
Soil bacterial community patterns
The rate of every microbial reaction
questions.explanation: It profiles bacterial community composition rather than measuring grain directly.
questions.source_section: High-throughput sequencing of soil community bacteria

questions.prompt: Why is a bacterial association not proof of causation?
options: Every bacterial sequence has the same function
Sequencing directly measures each treatment’s yield
Management differences may affect both microbes and yield
questions.explanation: Several changes can occur together across treatment systems.

questions.prompt: What do the scene’s microbe icons represent?
options: Conceptual symbols, not identified measured species
Measured relative abundances of the paper’s bacteria
A verified representation of bacterial growth rates
questions.explanation: The icons are invented teaching aids.
questions.source_section: High-throughput sequencing of soil community bacteria

visual_task: Choose maize, inspect the root-zone symbols and change the water stage or planting layout. Symbols are not measured bacteria, and the scene does not calculate crop yield.

title: Chemical waves in reaction-diffusion networks of small organic molecules

key_claims.text: The authors studied reaction–diffusion waves involving autocatalytic thiol chemistry and negative feedback in a hydrogel reactor.
Changing reactor geometry affected the observed wave behavior.
The authors used a reaction–diffusion model to analyze their chemical system.

limitations: The teaching simulation is a different abstract 1D model, not the paper’s full chemical kinetic model.
Its visual pattern, speed and parameters are not a fit to the reported reactor measurements.
learning_objectives: Explain why reaction and diffusion can produce a moving concentration pattern.
Identify the paper’s hydrogel and chemical feedback design.
Compare a conceptual simulation with an experimentally fitted model.

lesson_flow.title: Set up the experiment
lesson_flow.body: The researchers place a reaction network in a hydrogel with reagent supply and spatial transport. A concentration pattern can propagate without material moving as a solid object.
lesson_flow.check_question: What moves through the gel?

lesson_flow.title: Add feedback
lesson_flow.body: The network combines autocatalytic thiol chemistry with a negative-feedback reaction, linking local chemistry to the spread of reactants.
lesson_flow.check_question: How might local feedback differ from transport?

lesson_flow.title: Change geometry
lesson_flow.body: Experiments using different reactor geometries show that spatial arrangement matters to observed wave behavior.
lesson_flow.check_question: Why might geometry affect where a wave begins?

lesson_flow.title: Compare models
lesson_flow.body: The article uses a system-specific numerical model. The interactive scene uses a separate abstract 1D reaction–diffusion rule, so compare concepts rather than numerical wave speeds.
lesson_flow.check_question: Which assumptions would need checking before comparing speeds?

questions.prompt: What can spread through a reaction–diffusion system?
options: A concentration change coupled to reaction and transport
A fixed parcel of gel moving with the wavefront
A change in reactor shape traveling at the reaction speed
questions.explanation: A wave can be a propagating pattern in concentrations.

questions.prompt: What is the relation between the interactive model and the paper?
options: It contains the full fitted thiol reaction network
It is a distinct teaching model, not the full paper model
It reproduces the measured concentrations in the gel
questions.explanation: The toy model teaches the idea without claiming kinetic fidelity.

questions.prompt: Why investigate reactor geometry?
options: Geometry matters only when diffusion is absent
All reactor shapes have identical boundary conditions
Spatial boundaries and transport can change wave behavior
questions.explanation: The paper examined how geometry affected the observations.

visual_task: Change diffusion and reaction controls in the 1D model and compare patterns. Its species and parameters are abstract; it neither reproduces the paper’s detailed thiol kinetics nor predicts measured wave speed.

title: Experimental Study on the Kinetics of CO2 and H2O Adsorption on Honeycomb Carbon Monoliths under Cement Flue Gas Conditions
source_sections: Single and binary experiments (CO2, N2/H2O, and CO2/H2O)

key_claims.text: The researchers studied CO2 and water-vapor adsorption on honeycomb carbon monoliths under selected gas conditions.
They examined uptake kinetics with fitted models and compared materials and conditions.
Material and humidity affected results under the tested conditions, so no single ranking is guaranteed for all gas streams.

limitations: A finite-site teaching illustration is not a fitted adsorption capacity or the article’s complete kinetic mechanism.
The study uses particular materials and gas conditions; do not generalize its material ranking to every situation.
learning_objectives: Distinguish adsorption at a surface from bulk gas concentration.
Explain why humidity and adsorbent material are experimental variables.
Recognize that a toy site diagram does not establish the real microscopic mechanism.

lesson_flow.title: Define adsorption
lesson_flow.body: Molecules can accumulate at an adsorbent surface. The study compares honeycomb carbon monoliths exposed to carbon dioxide and water vapor.
lesson_flow.check_question: How does surface accumulation differ from gas concentration?

lesson_flow.title: Vary conditions
lesson_flow.body: The researchers tested gases individually and in mixtures under controlled conditions. Water vapor is relevant because a real flue-gas stream can contain moisture.
lesson_flow.check_question: Why compare a dry gas with a humid mixture?
lesson_flow.source_section: Single and binary experiments (CO2, N2/H2O, and CO2/H2O)

lesson_flow.title: Read uptake over time
lesson_flow.body: The article analyzes measured uptake kinetics and uses models to interpret them. Model parameters apply to the tested materials and conditions.
lesson_flow.check_question: What does a fitted curve need to be compared against?

lesson_flow.title: Limit the illustration
lesson_flow.body: A limited set of surface sites can help visualize shared occupancy, but it cannot establish exactly how these monoliths adsorb gas or predict their capacity.
lesson_flow.check_question: What experimental evidence would a numerical capacity require?

questions.prompt: Why include water vapor in experiments?
options: It fixes the same uptake rate in every carbon material
It can alter adsorption under the gas conditions studied
It replaces the need for single-gas experiments
questions.explanation: Humidity is a relevant variable in the article’s mixture experiments.

questions.prompt: Does an illustrative occupied-site count equal measured capacity?
options: Yes, because every site has the same measured energy
Yes, if the diagram shows a saturated surface
No; the site diagram is not fitted to the measured material
questions.explanation: Invented icons do not constitute an experimental adsorption measurement.

questions.prompt: What is adsorption here?
options: Accumulation of gas molecules at an adsorbent surface
Bulk mixing of gases without surface uptake
Condensation of all gas into a liquid reservoir
questions.explanation: The work studies uptake on carbon adsorbents.

visual_task: Choose CO2 or H2O in the surface-site illustration and inspect occupancy. Sites and binding are schematic; no capacity, kinetic fit or complete mechanism is inferred.

title: A Novel Si Nanosheet Channel Release Process for the Fabrication of Gate-All-Around Transistors and Its Mechanism Investigation

key_claims.text: The authors fabricated silicon and silicon–germanium multilayers and studied release of silicon nanosheets by removing the sacrificial material.
The authors compared release processes and investigated deformation using structural observations and simulation.
A multistep process improved the release in the reported experimental setting.

limitations: The teaching transistor is a generic conceptual model, not the paper’s multilayer fabrication process or TEM image.
Process measurements and simulated stress are different evidence types.
learning_objectives: Explain why a sacrificial layer can release a nanosheet.
Distinguish a gate-all-around architecture from an ordinary planar sketch.
Compare experimental structural observations with stress simulations.

lesson_flow.title: Build a stack
lesson_flow.body: The paper starts with alternating silicon and silicon–germanium layers. Removing the sacrificial material releases silicon sheets for a gate-all-around architecture.
lesson_flow.check_question: Which layer is intended to remain?

lesson_flow.title: Release carefully
lesson_flow.body: Etching and oxidation steps are organized to improve selective release. The problem is not merely to draw a channel but to preserve its shape and spacing.
lesson_flow.check_question: What could go wrong if sheets deform?

lesson_flow.title: Check the structure
lesson_flow.body: The article compares structural observations with simulation of stress during the process. Experimental imaging and simulated stress answer related but distinct questions.
lesson_flow.check_question: What does each source of evidence contribute?

lesson_flow.title: Connect to a basic transistor
lesson_flow.body: Use the generic transistor view to identify source, gate, channel and drain. It does not recreate the paper’s nanosheet fabrication or validate release quality.
lesson_flow.check_question: Which aspects of the nanosheet stack are absent from a generic transistor?

questions.prompt: Why remove a sacrificial SiGe layer?
options: To release silicon nanosheets
To remove the silicon sheets and retain SiGe
To convert the stack into a single bulk silicon layer
questions.explanation: Selective removal leaves the intended silicon sheets.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes experimental imaging from a stress simulation?
options: Both directly measure the stress field in the same way
Imaging observes structures while simulation estimates behavior under a model
Simulation replaces the need to inspect the fabricated stack
questions.explanation: These are complementary but different types of evidence.

questions.prompt: Does a generic transistor model reconstruct the paper’s etching process?
options: Yes, it implements the reported etching steps
Yes, its geometry was taken from the paper’s TEM scan
No; it illustrates a related device concept only
questions.explanation: The model is not a process simulation or a structural reconstruction.

visual_task: In the device view select nanosheet and identify gate and channels. The GAA diagram is conceptual, not a reconstruction of etching, deformation or measured nanosheet dimensions.

title: Vertical Silicon Nanowire Field Effect Transistors with Nanoscale Gate-All-Around

key_claims.text: The authors fabricated vertical silicon nanowire field-effect transistors with a nanoscale gate-all-around configuration.
They reported n-type and p-type devices and demonstrated a complementary inverter.
The device and inverter results are evidence for the particular demonstrated fabrication and measurements.

limitations: A planar educational transistor is not a geometrically accurate vertical nanowire.
The inverter view illustrates logic behavior, not the device’s measured switching curves.
learning_objectives: Identify a vertical nanowire and gate-all-around configuration.
Explain how complementary transistors can implement inversion.
Separate a logic truth table from measured device characteristics.

lesson_flow.title: Make the channel
lesson_flow.body: The article describes a vertical silicon nanowire transistor in which a surrounding gate controls a nanoscale channel.
lesson_flow.check_question: What is the geometric distinction from a flat channel?

lesson_flow.title: Compare devices
lesson_flow.body: The authors investigate both n-type and p-type devices and use complementary behavior to construct an inverter.
lesson_flow.check_question: Why do complementary devices provide useful switching paths?

lesson_flow.title: Trace a logic state
lesson_flow.body: In an idealized inverter, a low input corresponds to a high output, while a high input corresponds to a low output. Real devices also have nonideal transitions.
lesson_flow.check_question: What would a measured transfer curve add to this truth table?

lesson_flow.title: Check the model
lesson_flow.body: The interactive circuit is a conceptual inverter and does not reproduce the actual nanowire shape or measured transfer curve.
lesson_flow.check_question: Which device details would be needed for a physical reproduction?

questions.prompt: What surrounds the channel in the reported architecture?
options: Only the source contact
A gate in a gate-all-around arrangement
Only the drain contact
questions.explanation: The gate surrounds the nanowire channel.

questions.prompt: What is the output of an ideal inverter when the input is high?
options: High
Equal to the supply midpoint for both input states
Low
questions.explanation: An inverter reverses the logical state.

questions.prompt: What does the generic circuit not provide?
options: The article’s measured transfer curve
The conceptual relationship between input and output states
An illustration of complementary switching
questions.explanation: Its states are educational, not measured nanowire data.

visual_task: Select the nanowire device, then the inverter view; switch input 0/1 and compare the output. These diagrams are conceptual, not the paper’s measured nanowire or transfer curve.

title: A steep switching WSe2 impact ionization field-effect transistor
source_sections: Fabrication and working principle of WSe2 I2FET
Complementary inverter fabricated with WSe2 I2FET
Theoretical study of impact ionization characteristics

key_claims.text: The device uses WSe2 and an impact-ionization switching mechanism.
key_claims.source_section: Fabrication and working principle of WSe2 I2FET

key_claims.text: The paper demonstrates a complementary inverter using a p-type WSe2 impact-ionization device and an n-type MoS2 transistor.
key_claims.source_section: Complementary inverter fabricated with WSe2 I2FET

key_claims.text: The paper uses theoretical analysis to investigate its impact-ionization mechanism.
key_claims.source_section: Theoretical study of impact ionization characteristics

limitations: The generic CMOS inverter is prerequisite logic only, not a representation of the WSe2/MoS2 device or its avalanche mechanism.
It does not reproduce the article’s switching curves, materials or reported device performance.
learning_objectives: Identify the role of the two device types in a complementary inverter.
Explain inversion using input and output states.
Distinguish ideal logic from the paper’s physical switching mechanism.

lesson_flow.title: Study a different switch
lesson_flow.body: This study investigates an impact-ionization field-effect device based on WSe2. The authors describe a high-field ungated region in which energetic carriers create electron–hole pairs, multiplying carriers. This is not the generic silicon MOSFET mechanism.
lesson_flow.check_question: Which material and carrier process distinguish this device?
lesson_flow.source_section: Fabrication and working principle of WSe2 I2FET

lesson_flow.title: Build complementary logic
lesson_flow.body: The demonstrated inverter combines a p-type WSe2 impact-ionization device with an n-type MoS2 transistor. The paper’s Fig. 5 analyzes its measured inverting response.
lesson_flow.check_question: What is the functional role of an inverter?
lesson_flow.source_section: Complementary inverter fabricated with WSe2 I2FET

lesson_flow.title: Follow input and output
lesson_flow.body: In an ideal inverter a low input gives a high output and vice versa. Actual measurements describe the transition between states, not just the endpoints.
lesson_flow.check_question: What detail is absent from a two-state truth table?
lesson_flow.source_section: Complementary inverter fabricated with WSe2 I2FET

lesson_flow.title: Keep mechanisms distinct
lesson_flow.body: The generic CMOS inverter animation teaches prerequisite logic only; it does not simulate the paper’s WSe2 avalanche, MoS2, device characteristics or measured voltage response.
lesson_flow.check_question: What additional model would be needed to analyze the physical switching mechanism?
lesson_flow.source_section: Theoretical study of impact ionization characteristics

questions.prompt: Which pair appears in the reported complementary inverter?
options: Two p-type WSe2 impact-ionization devices
A conventional silicon CMOS pair only
A p-type WSe2 impact-ionization device and an n-type MoS2 transistor
questions.explanation: The paper combines devices of different materials and switching roles.
questions.source_section: Complementary inverter fabricated with WSe2 I2FET

questions.prompt: What can the simple circuit demonstrate reliably?
options: The ideal logical inversion relationship
The paper’s measured impact-ionization gain
The precise carrier distribution inside WSe2
questions.explanation: The generic view is intended for logic, not a materials simulation.
questions.source_section: Complementary inverter fabricated with WSe2 I2FET

questions.prompt: Why is a truth table incomplete device evidence?
options: It captures the complete transfer curve
It omits the measured transition and physical switching details
It measures the impact-ionization rate
questions.explanation: Real transfer characteristics contain more information than the ideal endpoints.

visual_task: Use the generic CMOS inverter as a prerequisite for understanding complementary logic: switch input 0/1 and compare the output. It is not the paper’s WSe2/MoS2 inverter, and it does not model carrier avalanche, its materials or the measured transfer curve.

title: Wafer-scale 2D MoS2 transistors with self-aligned angstrom gate length and nanometer channel length

key_claims.text: The authors report a vertical MoS2 device using a graphene edge as a very short gate electrode.
The article reports structural and electrical characterization of its fabricated devices.
The paper demonstrates transistor arrays and logic circuits at wafer scale in a research setting.

limitations: The generic transistor scene is not the paper’s vertical graphene-edge/MoS2 structure.
Demonstrated research arrays are not by themselves proof of commercial manufacturing readiness.
learning_objectives: Explain the basic role of gate and channel.
Identify the paper’s distinctive vertical material architecture.
Distinguish research demonstration from production-scale deployment.

lesson_flow.title: Identify the architecture
lesson_flow.body: The reported design uses a graphene edge as a very short gate electrode with a vertical MoS2 channel.
lesson_flow.check_question: How does this differ from a conventional planar sketch?

lesson_flow.title: Connect structure and evidence
lesson_flow.body: The authors characterize fabricated structures and electrical behavior; separate device simulation helps analyze mechanisms.
lesson_flow.check_question: Why do physical characterization and electrical measurements complement each other?

lesson_flow.title: Move beyond a single device
lesson_flow.body: The work reports wafer-scale arrays and logic circuit demonstrations, extending the evidence beyond an isolated transistor.
lesson_flow.check_question: What new integration questions arise in an array?

lesson_flow.title: Interpret cautiously
lesson_flow.body: A research demonstration does not alone establish manufacturing yield, reliability and commercial cost for all future products.
lesson_flow.check_question: Which additional evidence would commercialization require?

questions.prompt: What distinctive gate is used in the study?
options: The edge of graphene
A conventional polysilicon gate with a planar silicon channel
A metal gate around a silicon nanowire
questions.explanation: The vertical architecture uses a graphene edge as its gate electrode.

questions.prompt: Does a generic MOSFET scene reproduce that atomic geometry?
options: Yes, with the paper’s exact measured dimensions
No; it illustrates general gate and channel roles
Yes, it directly visualizes the graphene-edge TEM data
questions.explanation: The educational model is a general transistor diagram.

questions.prompt: What follows from a wafer-scale research demonstration?
options: Guaranteed commercial yield and long-term reliability
No further process validation is required
Evidence of demonstrated integration, with further validation needed
questions.explanation: Research integration and commercial readiness are different claims.

visual_task: Select the inverter view and switch input 0/1 to trace logic, or inspect the generic device. Neither view reproduces the paper’s materials, switching physics or measured devices.

title: Heterogeneous integration of 2D memristor arrays and silicon selectors for compute-in-memory hardware in convolutional neural networks
source_sections: System architecture and device heterogeneous integration

key_claims.text: The authors integrate two-dimensional HfSe2 memristors with silicon selectors in an array.
key_claims.source_section: System architecture and device heterogeneous integration

key_claims.text: The selector and memristor form one-selector-one-resistor cells; the selector helps address unwanted current paths.
The demonstrated neural-network workflow uses ex-situ training and array-based hardware evaluation.

limitations: A generic chip-stack illustration does not simulate the HfSe2 switching medium, selector or measured memory state.
The paper’s ex-situ training should not be described as training entirely on the chip.
learning_objectives: Distinguish a memory element from its selector in an array.
Explain why unintended current paths matter.
Describe the difference between ex-situ training and hardware inference.

lesson_flow.title: Combine technologies
lesson_flow.body: The paper combines HfSe2 memristor devices and silicon selectors in a heterogeneous array. Each component has a distinct role.
lesson_flow.check_question: Which component stores a resistance state?
lesson_flow.source_section: System architecture and device heterogeneous integration

lesson_flow.title: Understand the cell
lesson_flow.body: A one-selector-one-resistor cell combines a selector with a resistive memory element; the selector helps limit unwanted current paths in an array.
lesson_flow.check_question: Why might neighboring cells affect a read?

lesson_flow.title: Trace the workflow
lesson_flow.body: The neural-network weights are trained ex situ and evaluated through the reported hardware workflow. This does not mean all training happens on the device array.
lesson_flow.check_question: Where did training take place relative to the array?

lesson_flow.title: Use a schematic carefully
lesson_flow.body: A generic stack makes layered integration easier to picture but does not reproduce the paper’s selector physics, memristor states or array measurements.
lesson_flow.check_question: What evidence would be needed to model the actual cell?
lesson_flow.source_section: System architecture and device heterogeneous integration

questions.prompt: What is combined in the reported cell?
options: A silicon transistor and a floating-gate flash cell
A silicon selector and an HfSe2 memristor
A CMOS inverter and a volatile SRAM cell
questions.explanation: The study integrates a selector with a resistive memory element.
questions.source_section: System architecture and device heterogeneous integration

questions.prompt: What does ex-situ training mean in this workflow?
options: All gradient updates occurred inside each array cell
Training and inference were both omitted
Training occurred outside the hardware array
questions.explanation: The paper describes ex-situ training before hardware evaluation.

questions.prompt: What can the generic chip-stack view establish?
options: The conceptual idea of layered integration, not measured switching
The measured HfSe2 resistance of every paper device
The paper’s precise switching yield and voltage
questions.explanation: The stack is an illustrative model rather than measured device data.

visual_task: Choose the memristor view and compare SET, READ and RESET qualitatively. This fictional model does not reproduce the paper’s HfSe2/Ti device or measured voltages, selector physics or training.
